title: What happens when you run `jw ask`
subtitle: Following one question from your shell, through the `jw` wrapper, to a GPT worker and back

nodes.label: Your shell
nodes.simple: Where you type the command. It splits your words into arguments and starts the script.
nodes.deep: The shell does word-splitting and quote removal before `jw` ever runs, so `"where is auth handled?"` arrives as ONE argument (`$2`). Quoting here is what keeps the question in one piece.
nodes.analogy: The customer at the counter handing over a written order.

nodes.label: Command router
nodes.simple: Looks at the first word (`ask`, `run`, `review`...) and hands the rest to the matching function.
nodes.deep: A bash `case` on `${1:-}`. The `:-` default avoids an 'unbound variable' crash under `set -u` when you run `jw` with no args. `shift` drops the subcommand so each `cmd_*` sees only its own flags.
nodes.analogy: A switchboard operator routing each call to the right desk.

nodes.label: cmd_ask
nodes.simple: Reads the flags, wraps your question with safety rules, and asks `invoke` to run it.
nodes.deep: Parses `--cwd/--model/--timeout/--write` with a `while (($#))` + `case` loop. Unless `--write` is given, it appends a read-only constraint to the prompt. It always appends an anti-redraft line, then calls `invoke` with task name `ask-<timestamp>` and `JW_PRINT=full` so the full reply is printed.

nodes.label: invoke
nodes.simple: The engine room: runs jcode with a time limit, saves everything to disk, decides if it worked, and prints a short summary.
nodes.deep: Runs `jcode run ... --json` inside a subshell with `timeout`, stdout to `<task>.json`, stderr to `<task>.err`. Captures the exit code without tripping `set -e` (`|| rc=$?`). Extracts `session_id` and `text` with `jq`, classifies status (timeout / error / empty / ok), writes a ledger row, then prints either the full reply or just the EVIDENCE block.
nodes.analogy: A courier who delivers the letter, waits for the reply, files a copy, and reads you only the important part.

functions.name: status classification
functions.simple: Turns an exit code + reply into one word.

code.src:
local sid text status
  sid=$(jq -r '.session_id // empty' "$out" 2>/dev/null || true)
  text=$(jq -r '.text // empty' "$out" 2>/dev/null || true)
  if (( rc == 124 )); then status="timeout"
  elif (( rc != 0 )); then status="error($rc)"
  elif [[ -z "$text" ]]; then status="empty"
  else status="ok"; fi

nodes.label: jcode → OpenAI
nodes.simple: The actual AI agent. It reads your repo, thinks, and returns JSON with a reply and a session id.
nodes.deep: Invoked as `jcode run -p openai -m gpt-6-sol -C <cwd> --json <prompt>`. The jw script never talks to OpenAI itself; it only depends on two JSON fields: `.session_id` and `.text`.

nodes.label: Run files
nodes.simple: Every reply is saved in full on disk, so the terminal only needs to show a summary.
nodes.deep: `ask-<ts>.json` holds jcode's raw JSON; `ask-<ts>.err` holds stderr. `${out%.json}.err` is bash suffix-stripping: it removes `.json` from the end of the path.

nodes.label: Ledger
nodes.simple: A running log: one table row per run with time, task, model, session and status.
nodes.deep: `ledger_row` creates `ledger.md` with a header on first use, then appends with `>>`. For ad-hoc asks the slug is `adhoc`, so all asks share one ever-growing ledger.

code.src:
ledger_row() { # slug task model session status
  local dir="$ORCH_ROOT/$1"
  mkdir -p "$dir"
  if [[ ! -f "$dir/ledger.md" ]]; then
    printf '# Ledger: %s\n\n## jcode runs\n| time | task | model | session | status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n' "$1" > "$dir/ledger.md"
  fi
  printf '| %s | %s | %s | %s | %s |\n' "$(date '+%F %T')" "$2" "$3" "$4" "$5" >> "$dir/ledger.md"
}

traces.title: jw ask --cwd ~/app "where is auth handled?"
traces.trigger: You type `jw ask --cwd ~/app "where is auth handled?"` and press Enter.

steps.title: The shell builds the argument list
steps.simple: Your shell splits the line into 4 pieces and starts `jw` with them. The quotes keep your question as one piece.
steps.deep: After expansion `~/app` becomes an absolute path. Bash then starts the script; line 6 `set -euo pipefail` makes it stop on errors, on unset variables, and on failures inside pipes.

notes.6: The safety net for the whole script. `-e` exit on error, `-u` unset variable is an error, `pipefail` a pipe fails if any part fails.

steps.title: Route to cmd_ask
steps.simple: The router sees `ask` and calls `cmd_ask` with the remaining 3 arguments.
steps.deep: `shift` removes `$1`, so inside `cmd_ask`, `$1` is now `--cwd`. Unknown commands hit `*)` and `die` exits with code 2.

notes.257: `shift` throws away `ask`, then `"$@"` passes every remaining argument, each still correctly quoted.

steps.title: Parse the flags
steps.simple: A loop reads the arguments one at a time. Flags set settings. Anything else becomes the prompt.
steps.deep: `while (($#))` loops while arguments remain. Flags with a value do `shift 2`; the prompt does `shift`. Note: any second bare word silently REPLACES the prompt, because `prompt=$1` overwrites.

notes.229: `*) prompt=$1` overwrites, it does not append. `jw ask foo bar` asks only `bar`.

predict.q: You forget the quotes: `jw ask where is auth`. What prompt is sent?
options: An error about too many args
predict.why: Each bare word hits `*) prompt=$1`, overwriting the previous one. Only the last word survives, and no error is raised.

steps.title: Wrap the prompt with guardrails
steps.simple: Because you did not pass `--write`, jw adds a read-only rule to your question. It also asks for one final answer.
steps.deep: `(( write )) || prompt=...` runs the right side only when `write` is 0. These are prompt-level guardrails: the model is asked not to edit files, but nothing technically prevents it. The timestamp `ts` names the run files.

code.src:
(( write )) || prompt="$prompt

Constraints: read-only. Do NOT modify, create, or delete files; do not commit or push."
  prompt="$prompt

Give a single final answer; do not repeat or redraft it."
  local ts; ts=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
  JW_PRINT=full invoke adhoc "ask-$ts" "$model" "$tmo" "$cwd" "$ORCH_ROOT/adhoc/runs/ask-$ts.json" "$prompt"

notes.233: Arithmetic test: `(( 0 ))` is false, so the `||` branch runs and appends the constraint.

state.name: prompt
state.value:
"where is auth handled?"

Constraints: read-only. Do NOT modify... 

Give a single final answer...

steps.aside: A polite sign on the door, not a lock. Real isolation would need a sandbox or a read-only mount.

steps.title: Run jcode inside a time limit
steps.simple: jw starts jcode in your project folder, with a 15 minute limit. The reply goes to a file, errors to another file.
steps.deep: The `( ... )` subshell means `cd` does not change jw's own directory. `timeout 900` kills jcode after 900 s and returns 124. `|| rc=$?` is the key trick: under `set -e` a failing command would kill the script, but a command on the left of `||` is exempt, so the exit code is saved instead.

code.src:
invoke() {
  local slug=$1 task=$2 model=$3 tmo=$4 cwd=$5 out=$6; shift 6
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$out")"
  local rc=0
  (cd "$cwd" && timeout "$tmo" jcode run -p openai -m "$model" -C "$cwd" --json "$@") >"$out" 2>"${out%.json}.err" || rc=$?

notes.57: Three ideas in one line: subshell for `cd`, `timeout` for a hard limit, `|| rc=$?` to survive failure under `set -e`.

predict.q: jcode crashes with exit code 1. What does jw do next?
options: It saves rc=1 and keeps going
predict.why: `|| rc=$?` catches the failure, so `set -e` does not fire. jw continues, marks status `error(1)`, logs it, prints stderr and exits 3.

steps.title: The worker answers
steps.simple: jcode reads your repo, finds the answer and returns JSON with a `text` reply and a `session_id`.
steps.deep: jw relies on only two fields from jcode's JSON. That narrow contract makes jw robust to jcode adding new fields, but fragile if those two are ever renamed.

steps.title: Decide: ok, empty, error or timeout
steps.simple: jw pulls two fields out of the JSON and turns the result into one status word.
steps.deep: `jq -r '.x // empty'` prints nothing (not `null`) if the field is missing. `2>/dev/null || true` means a corrupt JSON file just yields empty strings instead of killing the script. The order of checks matters: timeout (124) is tested before generic errors.

code.src:
local sid text status
  sid=$(jq -r '.session_id // empty' "$out" 2>/dev/null || true)
  text=$(jq -r '.text // empty' "$out" 2>/dev/null || true)
  if (( rc == 124 )); then status="timeout"
  elif (( rc != 0 )); then status="error($rc)"
  elif [[ -z "$text" ]]; then status="empty"
  else status="ok"; fi

notes.62: 124 is the special exit code `timeout` uses. Checking it first gives a clearer status than `error(124)`.

steps.title: Log the run
steps.simple: One row is added to the ledger so every run can be found later.
steps.deep: The ledger row is written BEFORE the success check exits, so failed and timed-out runs are logged too. That ordering is what makes the ledger trustworthy for debugging.

steps.title: Print the summary and the reply
steps.simple: You see a short header, then the reply. The full JSON stays on disk.
steps.deep: Failure path: print the last 15 lines of stderr and exit 3. Empty reply: exit 4. For `ask`, `JW_PRINT=full` prints the first 100 lines of the reply. `run` uses the default mode and only prints the EVIDENCE block, which keeps an orchestrator's context small.

code.src:
echo "task:     $task"
  echo "model:    $model"
  echo "session:  ${sid:-none}"
  echo "cwd:      $cwd"
  echo "status:   $status"
  echo "output:   $out"
  if [[ "$status" != ok && "$status" != empty ]]; then
    echo "--- stderr (last 15 lines) ---"; tail -n 15 "${out%.json}.err" || true
    exit 3
  fi
  [[ "$status" == empty ]] && exit 4

  if [[ ${JW_PRINT:-evidence} == full ]]; then
    echo "--- reply (first 100 lines) ---"; printf '%s\n' "$text" | head -n 100
    return 0
  fi

notes.81: `JW_PRINT=full` was set on the same line as the `invoke` call in `cmd_ask`, so it applies only to that call.
notes.75: Anything except ok/empty is a failure: show stderr, exit 3.

whatifs.title: Remove `|| rc=$?`
whatifs.change: Line 57 becomes just the jcode command, without `|| rc=$?`.
whatifs.outcome: With `set -e`, any jcode failure or timeout now kills jw instantly. No ledger row is written, no status is printed and no stderr tail is shown. You get a silent exit and have to go digging in the .err file.
whatifs.lesson: Under `set -e`, catch expected failures explicitly so you can report them.

whatifs.title: Pass `--write` by habit
whatifs.change: You run `jw ask --write "..."` for every question.
whatifs.outcome: The read-only rule is no longer added. The worker may edit files directly in your working tree, not in a worktree. `jw run` isolates work in a git worktree; `ask` does not.
whatifs.lesson: Guardrails in prompts are soft. Isolation (worktrees) is the hard boundary.

whatifs.title: Two asks in the same second
whatifs.change: Two agents call `jw ask` at the same moment.
whatifs.outcome: Both compute the same `ts`, so both write `ask-<ts>.json` and `.err`. The later one overwrites the earlier one's files, while the ledger gets two rows pointing at one file.
whatifs.lesson: Timestamps with second precision are not unique ids.

decisions.title: Full output to disk, summary to screen
decisions.chosen: Save jcode's complete JSON to a file and print only a summary or EVIDENCE block.
decisions.simple: The header comment says why: keep the orchestrator's context small.
decisions.deep: Lines 3-4 state the goal. An orchestrating Claude session pays tokens for everything printed. Printing a summary and a file path lets it read the full reply only when needed.

alternatives.name: Print everything
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but every run floods the orchestrator's context and burns tokens.

alternatives.name: Print nothing, only the path
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest, but forces an extra read on every run, even when the summary would do.

decisions.title: Bash + jq instead of Python
decisions.chosen: A single bash script using `jq` for JSON.
decisions.simple: It mostly glues CLI tools together (git, timeout, jcode, flock), which bash does natively.
decisions.deep: `timeout`, `flock`, `git worktree` and exit codes are first-class in bash. The cost is sharp edges: quoting, `set -e` exemptions, and argument parsing done by hand.

alternatives.name: Python + argparse
alternatives.tradeoff: Safer argument parsing and real data structures, but more boilerplate around subprocess, timeouts and locking.

risks.title: Extra words silently replace the prompt
risks.what: `jw ask where is auth` sends only `auth`. There is no warning, so the answer can look plausible but be about the wrong thing.
risks.fix: Die if `prompt` is already set, or join all positional words.

risks.title: Missing flag value crashes with a cryptic error
risks.what: `jw ask --cwd` with nothing after it reads `$2`, which is unset. `set -u` aborts with `$2: unbound variable` instead of the usage text.
risks.fix: Check `(($# >= 2))` before `shift 2`, or use `${2:?--cwd needs a value}`.

risks.title: Run files can collide
risks.what: `ts` has one-second precision, so parallel asks can overwrite each other's output files.

quiz.q: Why does line 57 end with `|| rc=$?`?
options: To keep going after jcode fails
To retry jcode after a failure
quiz.why: `set -e` would abort on failure. Putting the command left of `||` exempts it and saves the exit code for the status logic.

quiz.q: Where would you look for the complete reply of an ask?
quiz.why: The ledger only stores a status row. The full jcode JSON is saved in the runs folder.

quiz.q: jcode runs past 900 s. What status does the ledger show?
quiz.why: `timeout` returns 124, which is checked first and mapped to `timeout`. Any non-ok, non-empty status exits 3.

quiz.q: What actually stops `jw ask` from editing files?
options: Only a sentence in the prompt
quiz.why: `ask` runs in your directory with a prompt-level constraint only. Worktrees are used by `jw run`, not `ask`.

glossary.def: A child copy of the shell, made with ( ... ). Changes inside it, such as cd, do not affect the parent.
Bash option: exit immediately when a command fails, except commands tested by if, &&, || and similar.
jw's markdown table of runs: time, task, model, session id and status.
A second working folder for the same git repo, on its own branch, so a worker can edit without touching your checkout.
